fields.h1: Build a Sign up Form for Any List You Run
fields.hero_description: Describe the sign up form and the limit on each choice. Emergent builds it, closes a choice the moment it fills and saves every sign-up to your own database.
fields.features_heading: Where Sign up Forms Usually Break
fields.features_subheading: Most sign-up trouble starts after the link goes out. Each piece below closes one gap, like nine people on a six-person shift.
fields.feature_1:
A cap on every slot or shift

Set a limit for each choice on the form. Once a choice fills, it closes, and the form shows only the options with room left. A cancellation hands that spot to whoever signs up next.
fields.feature_2:
Addresses confirmed before they count

Send each new subscriber a confirmation link and hold the address as pending until it is clicked. Pending rows expire on a schedule you set. Mistyped addresses never join the list.
fields.feature_3:
A roster everyone can check

Show parents who has signed up for each dish, by first name only, before they pick their own. You decide which columns the roster shows and which stay private to the organizer.
fields.feature_4:
Reminders and a link to cancel

Email each person their choice with a link to change it. Send a reminder the evening before, and alert the organizer in Slack when a slot is still short of people a day out.
fields.feature_5:
Every name synced to your other tools

Push each sign-up to HubSpot or any other tool with an API as it arrives. The record also stays in a database you own, where a developer can query it later on without an export.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain and your code

Publish the form on a custom domain or embed it on the site you already run. When a developer wants the sign-up flow inside your product, export the full code to a GitHub repo.

fields.usecase_heading: Sign up Forms for Four Different Crowds
fields.tab_content_1:
Six spots per shift, and a full shift closes

Eastside Pantry needs six people for each Saturday shift at its warehouse. Volunteers pick a shift and leave a phone number. Once the last spot goes, that shift drops off the form. Each volunteer gets a reminder email at 6:00 PM the evening before, and a cancellation reopens the spot.
fields.tab_content_2:
Subscribers who count only after they confirm

Readers of the Crumb Lane Bakery letter sign up with an email and pick topics such as weekend bread drops. Each new address gets a confirmation link and joins the list only once it is clicked. Confirmed readers are tagged by topic on their HubSpot contact. Rows still unconfirmed after seven days are deleted.
fields.tab_content_3:
No fifth dessert at the spring potluck

Parents at Maple Grove Elementary sign up to bring one dish to the spring potluck. Desserts stop at four. The next parent sees desserts marked full and picks another dish instead. Everyone can check the dish list before choosing, and the class coordinator gets the final list two days ahead.
fields.tab_content_4:
Teams of 50 or more go straight to sales

Tallyline opened its beta to a waitlist. The sign-up asks for a work email and team size, and every person gets a numbered place in line. A team of 50 or more is also posted to the sales channel in Slack with its company and headcount, where a rep picks it up.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Sign up Form
fields.howto_description: Count the choices and their limits first. The questions come last.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Name what people are signing up for
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Put a number on every choice
fields.howto_step_1_des: A volunteer shift and a newsletter need different records. Sketch one finished sign-up as a row before anything else: the person and the choice they made. Then note how you will reach them later, by email or by phone.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Note the cap for each option, like six volunteers per shift or four desserts. Then decide what a full option does. It can close, or it can start a waitlist that hands the next free spot to the first name on it.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Give each field a reader. The organizer needs a phone number for a shift, while a newsletter needs only an email. Make a question optional when only some people can answer it, and cut any question nobody will use.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Decide what each person receives and when: a confirmation right away, a reminder before the date and a note if their slot changes. Write that wording now, in the voice of the group that is sending it.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your notes in plain English, caps included, and say who gets alerted about new names. Emergent returns the form with its database and its emails. Change anything later by asking, such as adding a third shift or raising a cap to eight.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Sign up as a test person
fields.howto_step_6_des: Take a slot under a made-up name, then fill that option to its cap and watch it close. Cancel one test sign-up and check that the spot opens again. Fix whatever surprised you before the real link goes out.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Share it where people already look
fields.howto_step_7_des: Publish on your own domain or embed the form on a page your group visits. Post the link in a newsletter or on a printed QR code at the front desk. The roster shows which slots still need people as the date gets closer.

plan.angle: The top 10 splits between sign-up sheet services (SignUpGenius, SignUp.com, Grasshopper), template galleries (Jotform, Typeform, signupforms.com) and inspiration posts (Wisepops, Dribbble). Each sells either slots or a pretty email box. This page shows a sign up form as the gate to a list with a rule behind it: shifts that close at their cap, a newsletter that only counts confirmed addresses, a potluck that stops a fifth dessert, and a beta waitlist that sends big teams to sales. Every name lands in a database the organizer owns, and the FAQ answers the hyphen, Google Forms, HTML and template questions plainly.
tab_stories: A food pantry posts Saturday volunteer shifts with six spots each, closes a shift when it fills and emails each volunteer a reminder the evening before.
A bakery's newsletter form asks which topics a reader wants, adds an address to the list only after the confirmation link is clicked and tags the contact in HubSpot.
A school's end-of-year potluck caps each dish category, so once four desserts are claimed the next parent is offered sides or drinks instead.
A software startup's beta waitlist asks for a work email and team size, gives everyone a place in line and posts teams of 50 or more to the sales channel in Slack.
